chapters.html:
Castrum Kremnos was Strife.

It was an indisputable fact within the lands of Amphoreus – no one could disagree that the home of all things related to war and conflict was within those bloodied gates, for Kremnoans were known to be ferocious, drinking wines brewed from the blood of their enemies and fighting with lions in broad daylight to show their power.

Phainon didn’t have much of an appetite for blood, but he had once wrestled a wolf on the outskirts of Aedes Elysiae. That was close enough to a lion, right?

“No,” One of his companions grumbled, “Phainon, have you seen the size of a lion? Much less a Kremnoan lion?”

“Yeah, I get that, Caelus, but the wolf I fought was pretty big too,” Phainon reasoned, only to be met with a cackle from his other companion.

She turned to face them, walking backwards as she called out, “Phainon, your idea of big is peanuts to us.”

Then, as though she had made a funny joke, she said, “Although, you might have something big–”

“Stelle, not now!” Caelus groaned as he leapt forward to tackle his sister. They tussled for a bit, somehow still keeping pace with Phainon as they crossed the rocky terrain, and ended up with Caelus riding piggyback on Stelle as she carried on hiking as though nothing was wrong.

In his defence, Phainon hadn’t chosen to have such unconventional travel-buddies: they had accosted him at a tavern in Icatus on the night of the annual Georios festival, spouting nonsense about ‘meeting their meta-king’ and ‘needing his plot armour to help them get to Castrum Kremnos’. He had understood little of their ramblings, but Castrum Kremnos was on his list of places to visit as part of his expeditions, so he begrudgingly let them join.

They were surprisingly good companions, never complaining about rough conditions and being satisfied with meagre scraps for food, even going so far as to guard their scraps with a zealous passion. It mattered little to Phainon; it was no skin off his back.

“Phainon, are we there yet?” Caelus groaned into Stelle’s hair, only to recoil with a disgusted screech at something he tasted in that grey rat’s nest.

With Castrum Kremnos being a moving entity, it was impossible to gauge whether or not they were ‘there yet’. Still, Phainon did his best, using his boyish charms and charisma to wheedle information from pretty barmaids, gossipy old uncles and excitable young children. “Supposedly, we’ll see it once we pass that boulder over there.”

He raised a hand to point at the boulder, maybe fifty or sixty paces away, only to blink in surprise when he saw Stelle already halfway there. “Wha– wait up!”

It was truly remarkable how fast she could travel, even with her brother on her back, nimble like a mountain goat. But Phainon was no slouch either, and soon enough, the three of them were overlooking a lush green valley, and within the valley–

“Kremnos…” Phainon murmured.

“Doesn’t it look kinda empty?” Caelus propped his folded arms on Stelle’s head, frowning. “I mean, all the stories tell of a magnificent castle-colosseum within the city, but I don’t see anything.”

Stelle dumped him on the floor. “Idiot, don’t be xenophobic. Just because their magnificent castle-colosseum doesn’t meet your expectations–”

“I never said that! I only meant–”

“No, no, he’s right.” Phainon was also confused, looking down at the thriving city, but seeing nothing truly ‘magnificent’ about it. There were clusters of buildings, big and small, and the streets seemed bustling; yet there was a gaping vacancy at the head of the city, as though something were missing. But Kremnos was said to be a moving city, so perhaps they had to be frugal with their buildings in order to relocate easily?

He lifted the two siblings, one in each hand, and held them apart like squabbling kittens. It wouldn’t do them well to fight before even entering the city of strife. And so, carrying them like luggage under his arms – because it mustn't be forgotten, Phainon used to be a farmer and was more than capable of moving heavy things – he made his way down to the mountain.

A few citizens were going about their way on the path to the city, pausing to shoot him a friendly smile or a menacing stare, but overall, the journey to Castrum Kremnos was pretty anticlimactic.

“Do you think we’ll see a lion?” Stelle giggled maniacally, rubbing her hands together like some shady merchant from Dolos, “Do you think we’ll see their blood-wine?”

“I hope not, I brushed my teeth this morning,” Caelus snarked back. Did Phainon mention that his companions were a bit strange?

When they had reached the city’s gate, after finally putting his companions on the floor, a large, fearsome-looking man with streaks of white in his hair stared them down. Phainon tried to ignore the salivating glances Caelus was throwing his way. “State your names and business,” the man growled, folding his arms over his armoured breastplate.

Phainon hurried to introduce them, lest the siblings say something incriminating accidentally. “I am Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, and these are my companions, Stelle and Caelus.”

“From?”

“Um.”

“Don’t worry about it, big guy.” Stelle winked, trying and failing to look flirtatious. The man’s face twisted in a grimace.

“I am Krateros, a venerated general of the city; you will not address me as ‘big guy’.”

“Sure, big guy.”

Before the situation could escalate further, Phainon tossed Stelle over his shoulder. Then, for good measure, he tossed Caelus over his other. “My apologies, General Krateros. We are simply travellers, and we wanted to visit Castrum Kremnos, the renowned moving city of strife. Why, in my village alone, tales have been told of the fearsome warriors who feed on blood and–”

Krateros looked unimpressed. It seemed Phainon’s fancy words were not getting through to him.

“Ahaha, honestly, I’ve always wanted to visit,” Phainon offered. Perhaps he would be more receptive to the truth, “when I was little, I used to want to train here, and as I grew up, I just became fascinated with the culture.”

Krateros sighed and signalled a man to open the gates and let them pass. He turned on his feet, taking a few steps into the city before looking over his shoulder as if to say Well? Are you coming?

Phainon was not about to look such a wonderful gift-dromas in the mouth. He scurried forward, feeling a bit like a dromas himself with all the luggage (and people) he was carrying, and tried his best to meet Krateros’ domineering strides.

Castrum Kremnos was not what he had expected.

No lions were brawling with warriors in the streets, nor were there any breweries claiming to sell concoctions with blood, and the one time Phainon saw a person with red in his cup, the fragrant scent of pomegranates wafting out convinced him that perhaps the rumours about the city state were slightly exaggerated. They weren’t wrong about the people, though; that was for sure.

Children as young as three years of age ran around with wooden swords in hand, swinging at buildings and each other as if practising for their futures of pillaging. Unlike in some cities Phainon had visited, in which women were expected to be more docile and domestic, here, he could see babes suckling at the breast of seasoned warrior-maidens, toned with muscle and not made soft in motherhood. Fathers were firm, teaching the sword or partaking in hand-to-hand combat themselves as they grappled in little arenas, and young lovers sparred with each other in an uncommon form of courting.

That wasn’t to say the people were cruel, no, for the children darted to their parents with barely concealed glee and bragged about their spoils for the day, or cried in their laps for consolation after losing a duel with a neighbour. But it was obvious to Phainon, even for a traveller such as himself, that strife was prominent within the city.

“Not at all what you expected, eh?” A gruff voice, Krateros finally deigning to speak to Phainon. “Our women are strong and our men are eager for battle, yet somehow people decided that that meant we drink the blood of innocents.”

“I never thought that,” Phainon blurted out, and he jostled Caelus on his shoulder when he heard the man let out a sound of disbelief. “Do you guys move?”

“Excuse me?”

“People say Castrum Kremnos is a moving entity, but I wasn’t sure if that was yet another one of the rumours.”

Krateros paused – actually, just where was the man leading them? – to stroke his beard thoughtfully. Then his eyes lit up, a grunt of understanding escaping his lips as he brought Phainon to a door, labelled neatly with a sign reading ‘INN’.

“You'll want to find lodgings for the night,” he said matter-of-factly, “Kremnos gets notoriously warm, and you'll find yourself sweating like swine if you continue to carry your supplies around like that.”

He continued, not giving Phainon an opportunity to thank him, “as for your question. Well. You seem to have made a translation error.”

“What?” Phainon tilted his head, not unlike a confused dog. A translation error?

“In your search for such a moving entity, you must have been told about a ‘Castrum Kremnos’. But, in that phrase, ‘Castrum’ means ‘castle’.” Krateros explained, and suddenly it all made sense – the confusion when Phainon asked people from abroad about the moving city, the absence of a castle-colosseum when they spied the city from above.

“So you mean to say…”

“Yes. It is not the city that moves, but the castle.” Krateros pushed the door to the inn open and gestured for Phainon to go inside. “Our patron titan of Strife owns the castle and chooses where the castle will be, and it is considered an auspicious sign whenever Nikador returns to Kremnos.” At his command, a man standing behind the inn’s counter pulled out two sets of keys, laying them flat for Phainon to pick up. “It is said that when Nikador returns home, he stays here for ten days and heralds the start of the Kremnos Festival.”

Stelle coughed from where she had been tossed over Phainon’s shoulder, and he hurriedly dropped both her and Caelus to the floor. Oops, he had forgotten they were there.

Their faces were red from all the blood that had rushed to their heads, and Caelus rubbed at his sternum with a groan of discomfort. “Your farmboy strength is too crazy, man.”

“Never mind that,” Stelle interrupted, “what does the Kremnos Festival mean?”

It seemed that that was the right question to ask, for Krateros puffed up proudly and took a seat on one of the klines situated in the hotel’s foyer, beckoning the trio to gather round him like he was a wizened old grandfather on a winter’s day.

“The Kremnos Festival is a competition between the greatest swords of our people. Every year, Nikador returns home during the summer months, and under the blazing light of Aquila’s gaze, we fight for valour in the castle arena, with our titan as a witness. For warriors, the Festival is a chance to prove themselves in combat, but it is also the most auspicious time for marriage, setting off on conquest, and even for a child to be conceived.”

Violent coughing broke out at his last words. “I’m sorry?” Phainon choked, thumping at his chest as if that would fix his confusion, “You said… a child to be conceived?”

Krateros gave a resolute huff, “Outlanders may view such matters as unseemly for discussion, but here in Kremnos, we honour the fertility bestowed upon our people by Nikador's presence. We encourage copulation during the Kremnos Festival, for even men can–”

“Right, right.” This conversation seemed to be derailing a little.

The sun was starting to waver in the sky, cornflower blue melting in the soft lilac of twilight, and more and more people were filtering into the inn with baggage in hand. It would be best for them to search for a place to eat, and then get settled in for the night before it was too late.

With a few final words of information, Krateros was off to do whatever generals did, and then it was just Phainon, Caelus and Stelle perched in a circle in the inn’s crowded foyer.

“Well,” Stelle turned to Phainon with a glint in her eye, her twin copying her perfectly, “I'm kinda hungry.”

In the middle of the night, the raucous growl of Phainon's stomach woke him up, and the hollow feeling of hunger was what encouraged him to slip off of the shitty kline he had been delegated to sleep on instead of one of the two, perfectly reasonably sized beds.

(“You can't sleep on my bed, I'm a lady,” Stelle had scoffed as she looked him up and down.

Caelus only batted his eyes, covering his chest with his hands and trying to appear like a dishevelled maiden. “W-well, I guess you can sleep in my bed… but kyaaa~ who will ever marry me then!?”

Phainon took the kline.)

Late at night, there was not a single stall or eatery open for business, and the streets looked completely devoid of life. If Phainon still believed in paltry childhood stories, he might've thought that the whole city had been placed under a sleeping spell strong enough to make people snore through storms and invasions, and only he, as the honourable chosen hero, was too powerful to fall victim to such a spell.

Obviously, he was too old for those kinds of tales.

Yet as he made his way through the desolate streets, no food in sight, he was beginning to lose hope.

Should he just snack on one of their travel rations? But dried fish and crackers didn’t sound that appetising at the moment, he wanted something meaty, something juicy and plump for him to suckle and chew on while his head was encircled by a pair of powerful thighs that he could–

Oh.

Maybe he was a little bit horny as well.

But in Phainon’s defence, many of the features he was attracted to could be spotted easily in Kremnos – muscular bodies, sharp eyes, straw-coloured hair that shimmered under the sun, tattooed warpaint tracing over tanned skin. He hadn’t seen anyone fully encompass his ideal type, but that was not to say that the Kremnoan people weren’t quite attractive.

As much as he wanted to feast in between someone’s legs, however, there was no chance of that happening in the current state of the city, unless he saw some ethereal nymph wandering around, entreating him to chase.

Phainon looked around him. No nymphs in sight.

His next option, therefore, would have to be hunting down a wild swine and cooking it over a spit.

In Aedes Elysiae, the notorious ‘Phangry’ could often be seen prowling through the nearby forests in hunt, scaring the balls off of Galba whenever they ran into each other.

Phainon only did so to provide for his family, understanding of the fact that he tended to eat most of the food in the village when his hunger overtook his brain. If he brought back his own game, then at least he gave his family a chance to eat too.

In any case, he had experience tracking down wild swine, of which he had seen a few in the forest on the outskirts of Castrum Kremnos, so it should be easy for him to make a quick meal to sate the growing pit in his stomach.

Phainon proceeded forward to the forest, passed through the gap for the moving castle, and entered the thick woods. In the distance, there was a strange clanking noise, like an enormous machine was traversing through the valley.

The tracks in front of him were abnormally large, though they were undoubtedly boar tracks. It didn’t matter, Phainon was in Castrum Kremnos, and everyone said that ‘Castrum Kremnos was Strife’, so fighting a boar would be like a show of his strength. Yeah. It had nothing to do with the prospect of an even larger meal than if he had found a common pig.

An enraged screech echoed through the forest and scared the clusters of birds off of their nests and causing Phainon to look up, alert.

Before him was a boar the size of a house, covered in brown fuzz and with curved tusks that looked as sharp as Phainon’s sword. It had beady little eyes that watched him with anger, hot air puffing out of its snout as it inhaled the scent of its prey.

But what it didn’t know was that it was Phainon’s prey.

The boar was easy to subdue – with its sheer size, Phainon could easily misdirect it through the trees, and cause it to topple over in confusion after one too many times bumping into a tree, allowing him to toss his trusty net over it.

“Caelus said it was a scam,” Phainon huffed as he tied up the boar, “Caelus said that the lady selling this in Dolos was nothing but a trickster. Ha, who’s the trickster now?”

The boar looked at him in disbelief. Whatever, Phainon was going to eat it.

And then they heard it, a resounding clang as something hit the ground, shaking the very foundations they were standing on with reverberations from the impact.

Phainon abandoned the boar in place, ignoring its second enraged screech of the night to rush out of the forest and towards the noise, towards the city. But then his footsteps slowed, until he stopped in his tracks as the thicket of trees faded out into the empty space at the head of Castrum Kremnos. The empty space, which was now filled.

Nikador had returned home.

It was magnificent.

Marbled pillars of white spiralled to the sky, gilded and glimmering under the pale moonlight like heaps of precious gold. Each archway, a gaping maw in the stone, seems to swallow the light and cast deep, cavernous shadows, yet the gargantuan sword hovering over the circular arena illuminated the castle with its powerful glow. The very air around it felt heavy, charged with the echoes of a million voices – the roar of a crowd, the clanging of steel, the desperate cries of vanquished warriors.

On shaky feet, Phainon approached the imposing gate, engraved with ancient Kremnoan words and adorned with the stone head of a lion baring its fangs in a silent roar.

Incredible. He had to go inside.

In hindsight, perhaps he was delirious from hunger, for he did not normally make a habit of trespassing on royal territory. But something about the castle called out to him, beckoning him to plunder those walls and stake a claim on the land.

He hadn’t specified whether his delirium was from physiological hunger or carnal.

“Who dares trespass?”

A booming voice, smooth and deep as it commanded a response. Phainon couldn’t see anyone around him, though, completely isolated outside the imposing castle.

“You are no Kremnoan,” the voice scoffed, and the vibrations of sound caused the air around them to feel charged. “Why are you here?”

“Who am I speaking to right now?” Phainon didn’t want to question this omniscient voice, but he found it hard to hold a good conversation if he didn’t have something to focus his gaze on. Slowly, he trailed his eyes along the front of the castle, stopping at the gate.

The stone lion head stared at him. Could that be it?

“Are you the lion?” he asked, peering closer at the sharp fangs in its mouth. Goodness, Kremnoan lions looked ominous.

He only received a mocking scoff.

“Well, that’s not very nice,” Phainon huffed, “you could just say no, instead of–”

A large shadow fell over him, blocking out the moonlight and blanketing the entire gateway as a gargantuan hand, gloved in a dangerous-looking gauntlet, reached down and plucked Phainon from where he was standing, raising him high above the pillars of the castle like he was nothing more than a fly knocking on the doors.

The hand, as Phainon was steadily realising, belonged to a man who towered over the castle, haloed in moonlight with feathery hair the colour of the wheat fields back home and leonine eyes that swept over him in a golden gaze. Letting his eyes wander further, Phainon saw that the giant man’s beautiful face was connected to an even more beautiful torso, lazily leaning his face on his other hand while displaying his dusky nipples on great, voluptuous breasts that rose and fell with each breath.

As Phainon watched those soft mounds, entranced by the decadent necklace adorning them and the red tattoos creating a path for him to trace with his tongue – if he were of a similar size to the giant, at least – he found himself salivating slightly.

From where he was dangling in the man’s pinched hold on the back of his tunic, Phainon felt like an ant.

He liked it.

“I’ll ask you again,” the giant said, drawing Phainon’s attention to his plush pink lips, “who are you, and why have you come here?”

Phainon swallowed and spoke. “I am Phainon, of Aedes Elysiae, here on account of my travels.” Before the giant had a chance to retort, his eyebrows already furrowing in confusion, Phainon continued, “I was told that the castle moved, but no one ever enlightened me of such a magnificent creature residing within its walls.”

There. He had shown his hand, signifying his blatant desire for the giant – now it was up to him to choose what to do.

“‘Creature’?” The giant huffed in offence, “You dare call me something so primitive?”

No! That was the wrong reaction!

The giant narrowed his sun-like eyes and brought Phainon closer to his face.

Ok, Phainon could get behind this reaction.

“I’m much bigger than you, you know,” the giant murmured, his voice like rolling thunder as his warm breath puffed out, “I could eat you, and not even need to chew.”

“Please do.”

Phainon didn’t mean to say that. He meant to say, ‘No, don’t eat me, Mr Beautiful Giant, hahaha,’ and hopefully convince the blond to agree to be his wife by impressing him with his svelte nature so they could go and make love under the stars and have lots of kids, but unfortunately, he was a little distracted.

Below, dusty brown nubs and heavy tits called his name. Above, a captivating face twisted in disgust. Which to look at? Decisions, decisions.

There was a whoosh of air as Phainon felt himself moving through the sky, and soon enough, his feet were back on solid ground, far from the entrance of the castle and free to drink in the sight of the giant in all his glory.

A truly splendid being, even from afar. But Phainon mourned the distance that had been placed between them; however, at least from here, he could see the man in more detail.

He was chained to the castle, with layers and layers of interlocking metal links draping over him, some of the ends trailing out beyond the confines of the castle. Perhaps he was a threat; perhaps he wore those chains himself to appear threatening. To Phainon, it didn’t matter: he looked more like one of the dancers at a pub in Dolos, scantily clad in ribbons to accentuate the fullness of their figures and accrue more tips.

As though sensing the lewd thoughts coursing through his mind, the giant’s face pinkened. “Shameless human–”

“Now that I’m all the way over here,” Phainon called out, yelling so the giant could still hear him, “will you at least tell me who you are?”

“There’s no need to shout, I can hear you just fine.”

The giant shifted, his mountainous form settling in a more relaxed sprawl as he leaned his head on folded arms that settled on the top of the castle. He looked less like a spoiled king like this, and more like a siren peeking over the edge of a boat to entrap a sailor, or a curious lover.

Maybe not so much a ‘lover’, but Phainon was biased.

“I am Strife.” The giant said, his tone bored as he watched Phainon with tentative eyes. His gorgeous hair had fallen forward, miles of blond strands covering the gilded bannisters.

“Strife,” Phainon said dimly, “you’re… Nikador.”

The giant's brow pinched, but he jerked his head in a nod. Phainon tried not to look at the way that movement caused his chest to bounce slightly.

“Why would the titan of Strife be chained to his castle?” He questioned aloud. It made no sense to Phainon for such a powerful being to be limited to a domain as constrictive as a castle. How was Nikador supposed to go out and oversee wars if he was stuck in his amphitheatre?

Another scoff. “I am not chained to the castle, I am the castle.”

“What.”

Nikador rolled his eyes,“‘Castrum Kremnos is Strife.’ Have you never heard those words?”

Oh. Yet another mistranslation, it seemed. From what Phainon now understood, most of his childhood dreams and favourite myths revolved around Castrum Kremnos, the castle, and not Kremnos the city-state. And when people spoke of it being strife, they were not speaking of strife, but Strife. Easy mix-up.

“Are you sure you’re Nikador and not Mnestia,” Phainon blurted out, “because you’re gorgeous.”

He didn’t mean to say that. He had meant to ask if the titan was willing to take him on as an apprentice, so that he could train under him (and on top of him, if he was lucky), and get stronger so he could travel through Amphoreus and save those in need. After all, it was Phainon who stood before him, the only person in this city not ensnared by sleep.

The titan looked unamused at his compliment. He glared at Phainon.

“You look just as beautiful when you glare. Can I be yours?”

Nikador sputtered, his flush darkening in a strangely cute way for a man of his size. “Cease your incessant words, you–”

“Nikador,” Phainon interrupted, “may I court you?”

The titan paused and frowned. “Don’t call me that,” he finally muttered, and then a gauntlet-covered hand was rising to cover the lower half of his face, feline eyes looking away as he mumbled, “...I’m Mydeimos.”

“Oh? So you’re not Nikador?”

Phainon watched with barely concealed glee as the titan dropped his hand, revealing his lips unconsciously pursed in a pout. “Nikador is… a title. If you wish to court me, then you shouldn’t call me by my title.”

Clearly, Phainon’s weak attempts at flirting were managing to win over the titan. In Aedes Elysiae, courting spanned for a minimum of half a year, in which both parties had to prove themselves as capable partners for each other, able to withstand the changing seasons while still fostering romance.

For a titan, half a year was nothing. But Phainon was nothing if not dedicated.

“I see, my dear Mydei,” He was taking a risk by calling the titan by a nickname, but he couldn’t help himself. “Then, are you hungry?”

“Huh?” Mydei tilted his head, conveniently unblocking the moon from behind him. “I guess so, I was travelling for a while…”

With a quick request for the titan to not go anywhere, Phainon darted back into the forest. If he had secured the netting right, it should still be… there!

He grabbed the boar by its bound legs, ignoring its indignant screeches, and began tugging it back to his lovely Mydei. Phainon didn’t have the facilities to cook the boar or slaughter it, but surely in such a sprawling castle, Mydei would be able to prepare them a meal. Then, he could lean back and place Phainon right on the swell of his breasts as they ate together, allowing them a peaceful moment of repose in the quiet night.

The idea sounded brilliant!

“Mydei, I have brought you a gift!” Phainon chirped, and he hauled the flailing boar forward with ease. He needed to prove himself to be a powerful suitor for the titan; otherwise, he might not be taken seriously.

Mydei’s lips parted. His jaw dropped. “Wha–? Just… where did you get that boar from?” His voice was stunned, the rich cadence reaching Phainon’s ears and creating a wonderful reprieve from the erratic noises of the boar.

He stretched an arm forward, the movement as elegant as a tree swaying in the wind yet as decisive as a tidal wave, and lifted the boar. In his hands, the boar was about the size of a pomegranate – it filled his palm yet was not big enough to escape it.

Phainon let out a proud laugh. “I tracked it down in the forest and caught it.”

He didn’t need to say too much, but the simple tone with which he spoke should be enough to convince Mydei that he would make a capable husband. After all, this huge boar was a testament to his ability to provide his wife with food, and if he could catch one, then he could catch enough to satisfy the titan’s potentially voracious appetite.

“Hm.”
